transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-07
Time: 09:00 PT / 17:00 BST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Clara (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Priya (Starlight Head of ML), Marcus (Infra), Avery (PM)

Summary:
Short: kickoff POC scoping for quality gates and load/benchmark runbook. Focus: golden prompts, regression tests for hallucination/formatting, acceptance thresholds, and sizing for a dedicated test run. Customer emphasized strong SLAs for formatting (CSV/JSON outputs) and low hallucination rate for financial extraction use-case.

Topics: success criteria, golden prompt corpus, len/dist of real traffic, regression test automation, scoring rubric, hallucination detection, rollout timeline, infra/network constraints, security checklist.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Clara (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Hi Priya, Marcus, Avery. We wanted to use this time to map out the quality gate for the POC and what a benchmark estate looks like. Jonas and I will run point on the tech side.
[00:27] Priya (Starlight): Great thanks. We basically need to validate two things: one is extraction fidelity from unstructured docs — fields must be correct and formatted for our downstream ETL, and two is that the model doesn't hallucinate regulatory statements. Those two are blockers for product.
[00:47] Jonas (Redwood SE): Totally. When you say extraction fidelity, is that strict schema-enforcement, or are you okay with a verification step? Like do you require perfect CSV rows out of the box, or do you want a human-in-the-loop guardrail?
[01:05] Priya: For stage one we need near-perfect formatting. Our pipeline expects date fields as YYYY-MM-DD, numeric amounts normalized, and a set of enumerated categories to match our taxonomy. We can tolerate a small number of verification edits but the acceptance criteria has to be deterministic so downstream systems don't break.
[01:25] Avery (PM): To add, SLA side: if more than 1% of rows need manual touch, the integration path becomes costly. So success metric is something like <1% formatting failures, and hallucination rate under X — we'll define X in the session.
[01:45] Marcus (Infra): Also we have network constraints when talking about a private pilot. Our firewall and peering require specific egress IPs and an approval window for the VPC peering. We'll need Redwood's VPC deployment checklist early.
[02:04] Clara: Noted — we'll attach that in the security docs pack. On hallucination, we've got a couple strategies: golden prompt anchoring, retrieval-augmented responses (RAG) so the model cites context, and an automatic hallucination classifier that looks for contradiction to provided evidence. For this POC we usually run a mixture: golden prompts + regression tests + human spot-check.
[02:35] Priya: Can you explain the golden prompt idea — how do you pick them?
[02:42] Jonas: Sure. Golden prompts are representative input-output pairs that capture the edge cases and typical cases from your workload. We curate ~150-300 golden prompts across categories: short forms, long narratives, noisy OCR text, and adversarial cases. We also include negative examples that intentionally probe hallucination (e.g., ask for nonexistent fields).
[03:06] Priya: 150 to 300 — that seems high. Is that required?
[03:10] Jonas: It's not strictly required, but it helps to get statistically meaningful regression signals across sub-categories — date parsing, currency normalization, enum mapping, and hallucination checks. You can start with a smaller warm-up set (~50) then iteratively add.
[03:26] Avery: For scoring what metric do you usually use? Accuracy? F1? Something custom?
[03:32] Jonas: We do both exact-match for strict formatting fields and fuzzy metrics for semantic fields. Example: for dates and enums we do exact-match. For free text extraction we use F1/token-level overlap plus a hallucination score — a binary flag if extraneous entity appears. We then compute a composite score: 0.6 formatting + 0.4 hallucination tolerance, or you can weight it differently.
[03:58] Priya: We need the composite to be strict on hallucination — a single hallucinated regulatory clause is a showstopper. Can that be a hard fail rather than a weighted score?
[04:09] Clara: Yes, we can set hard gates. For instance: any hallucination detected in the golden set => fail; otherwise apply composite scoring. Many enterprise POCs use a two-tier gate: hard-pass on hallucination and soft pass on formatting thresholds.
[04:23] Marcus: How do you detect hallucination programatically?
[04:27] Jonas: Several ways: 1) RAG with source attribution — if model outputs a statement that isn't supported by the retrieved context we flag it. 2) Named-entity cross-checks against the source document; if an entity not present is introduced, it's suspicious. 3) Trained hallucination classifier — simple binary classifier trained on output diffs, but that needs labeled examples.
[04:49] Priya: For our use-case the RAG approach is appealing because we already keep canonical documents. But retrieval latency and token budget matter.
[04:58] Jonas: Good point. That's where model choice and batching interplay with cost. We'll recommend a model variant with retrieval-friendly context windows and a quantized variant for cost. We can also use prefix-KV caching for repetitive prompts to reduce per-token compute.
[05:15] Avery: This is getting into performance. For the benchmark run, what load should we simulate? Our traffic is bursty; typical sustained QPS is ~12 with spikes to 150 for 45 seconds during batch imports.
[05:29] Jonas: We'll need your trace to size the run. For the lab run we suggest two phases: functional correctness at low QPS (to validate gates) and then scaled load test using dedicated nodes to reproduce your spike profile. For sizing: we'll propose a 1-hour spike run that simulates 150 QPS with average sequence length 450 tokens and 99th percentile latency target of X — we'll define X with you.
[05:52] Priya: Our internal SLO is 95th < 400ms and 99th < 800ms for single-call end-to-end extraction. Can Redwood meet that on dedicated?
[06:03] Jonas: On dedicated we can get there, depends on model size and quantization. For example, a 13B quantized model with optimized kernels usually hits ~350ms 95th on A100-equivalent infra for the seq lengths you quoted; we'll share benchmark numbers.
[06:20] Marcus: For private deployment we might have older GPUs, which will change latency. We might need a compatibility plan for mixed infra.
[06:29] Clara: We can include a model compatibility matrix and fallback policy in the runbook: if private GPUs can't meet latency, we route to a hosted-safe fallback that maintains lower latency but higher cost. That routing policy is part of Redwood’s smart routing capabilities.
[06:45] Priya: Ok, back to quality tests — what does a regression suite look like?
[06:50] Jonas: Typical regression suite has three buckets: golden prompt corpus (deterministic expected outputs), fuzz/edge-case generator (randomized permutations to probe formatting/parsing), and adversarial probes (crafted to cause hallucination or format breaks). We recommend automated scoring pipeline that runs nightly against any new model or config change. For POC we run baseline + two candidate models and compare regressions.
[07:16] Avery: How do you handle tokenization mismatches? We saw weird splits for our proprietary product names.
[07:22] Jonas: Tokenization can cause downstream errors. We recommend normalizing tokens at the prompt layer (explicitly pass canonical forms) and include tokenizer-aware checks in the regression suite. Also blacklist/whitelist terms in post-processing for extraction pipelines.
[07:38] Priya: What about hallucination thresholds — can you give an example pass/fail?
[07:42] Jonas: Example: In golden corpus of 200 prompts, zero hallucination allowed; in live-sim (sample of 10k) we allow hallucination <= 0.1% for non-regulatory fields, 0% for regulatory/legal fields. Formatting failure must be <1% across the sample.
[07:59] Priya: Sounds reasonable. We'll push for 0% for anything that touches regulatory text.
[08:06] Clara: Noted. We'll codify that in the acceptance criteria.
[08:10] Marcus: For the runbook — will you provide scripts and a reproducible infra template?
[08:15] Jonas: Yes. The runbook will include: terraform snippets for dedicated nodes, definitions for workload generator (k6 + custom prompt feeder), a benchmark spreadsheet template with per-prompt metrics, and a CI job that runs the regression suite.
[08:29] Priya: Great. On scoring in the spreadsheet, please include per-prompt fields: exact_match, f1, hallucination_flag, latency_ms_p95, memory_peak_mb.
[08:40] Jonas: We'll include those columns. Also add columns for 'context_source_match' (boolean) to validate RAG citations.
[08:48] Avery: Who will run the initial benchmarking? Redwood or Starlight?
[08:52] Clara: Usually Redwood runs the first functional pass with your sample data on a Hosted testbed, then we co-run the large-scale spike tests with dedicated nodes in your environment or in a dedicated Redwood environment with peered VPC. We prefer to run the heavy-lift with Redwood SEs present so we can tune kernels/quantization live.
[09:10] Priya: For regulatory reasons we prefer the dedicated run to be within our VPC. We'll need a short list of required permissions and the peering window.
[09:18] Marcus: We'll also need to know expected egress and storage for the benchmark logs. That affects approval timelines.
[09:24] Clara: We'll provide an estimate in the next 48 hours.
[09:27] Priya: One more on eval: can Redwood help set up automated hallucination labeling? We don't have labeled hallucination examples.
[09:34] Jonas: We can seed the classifier with examples from your golden prompts and a curated public corpus. For higher accuracy you'll want human-labeled examples — we can propose a small labeling run of ~1,000 examples to bootstrap.
[09:48] Priya: Cost for labeling?
[09:50] Clara: We'll include a pricing ballpark in the follow-up. For the POC we often offer a small labeling credit.
[09:58] Avery: Timeline wise — how long to get to a demoable POC with metrics?
[10:03] Jonas: Typical cadence: week 0 (now) scoping and data collection; week 1 seed golden prompts + host functional run; week 2 focused regression improvements and two candidate models; week 3 dedicated spike run and final report. So about 3 weeks to demoable results if we get traces and prompts on time.
[10:23] Priya: That speed is good. We'll aim to hit those dates.
[10:27] Marcus: Any known gotchas?
[10:29] Jonas: A few: mismatched character encodings in OCRed text (introduces weird tokens), proxies that drop long streaming responses, and drift between dev prompt templates and production prompts. We'll put checks for all three in the runbook.
[10:44] Priya: For acceptance, besides the numeric gates, can we have an operational rollout plan? For example, a canary percent and automatic rollback trigger?
[10:52] Clara: Yes — Redwood supports canary rollouts with A/B and automatic rollback on defined regression alerts. We can include a recommended rollout: 1% -> 10% -> 50% with regression checks running at each step and automated fallback to the previous model on failure.
[11:06] Avery: Last thing: documentation and handoff. After POC we need a runbook that's readable by our on-call engineers.
[11:12] Jonas: We'll deliver a runbook with 'how to reproduce', 'how to interpret spreadsheet', 'alerting thresholds', and 'kernel/quantization tuning notes'. We'll also run a 2-hour handoff session for ops.
[11:24] Clara: Ok I'll summarize the next steps in the follow-up email. Anything else?
[11:29] Priya: No, that covers it. Looking forward to the benchmark template.
[11:33] Marcus: We'll start working on the trace export and firewall dates.
[11:36] Avery: Thanks all.
[11:38] Clara: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

Recap (auto):
- Acceptance: 0% hallucination for regulatory fields on golden set; formatting errors <1% sample; allow <=0.1% hallucination for non-regulatory in large sample.
- Golden prompts: start with 50 seed prompts, expand to 200 across buckets.
- Regression suite: nightly CI job with exact match/f1/hallucination/latency metrics.
- Load tests: functional low-QPS pass, then 1-hour spike run at 150 QPS with avg seq length ~450 tokens.
- Deliverables: benchmark spreadsheet, runbook, terraform snippets, SOC2 + VPC checklist, model compatibility matrix, and a 2-hour handoff session.
